I am not a believer in glue work 1 . Processes that can only be sustained by the unrewarded sacrifice of engineers ought to die.

Now that LLMs are writing most of our code, does that free human engineers up to do more glue work ? No, it doesn’t. I think glue work is actually less important to companies than it was in the 2010s. Let’s go through four reasons why.

First, AI decreases the amount of coordination needed to ship . The magnifying effect of AI agents means that any single engineer can now take on projects that would previously have needed a small team. A lot of glue work was helping with coordination: booking kickoff and status meetings, passing around internal updates, and so on. A single engineer doesn’t need to do any of that.

Second, engineers in the 2020s require less “careful handling” . In my experience, the most important subcategory of coordination-based glue work was managing difficult people . Many companies have secret gatekeepers: engineers with outsized influence and large egos who will shoot down your project if they feel insufficiently consulted. I’ve written before about how some teams are structurally set up to be gatekeepers, and how some engineers could get by in the 2010s by basically saying no to everything . The end of ZIRP changed all that. Many of the prickliest gatekeepers have been forced out of the industry or coerced into changing their attitude, which reduces the amount of necessary glue work required to ship.

Third, people are hiring fewer juniors . This is probably a bad thing for the industry, but it does also eliminate a big category of glue work. Experienced hires need less hand-holding, so companies don’t need people to quietly volunteer to onboard new hires.

Fourth, write-only reports can be automated with LLMs . A lot of glue work was what I call “proof of work” : writing a report to demonstrate that you’re aware of what your team is doing, or filling in a template to satisfy some legal requirement. This was often work that nobody wanted to do, so it relied on someone volunteering to “be glue”. Now reports like these can be quickly turned out with LLMs. It doesn’t really matter that nobody wants to read LLM text, because the point of these reports was never to be read anyway.

Can LLMs just automate all glue work? Absolutely not. Many engineers are trying to do this out of a kind of manic optimism, but it’s a really bad idea. Write-only reports are one thing, but communicating to other engineers cannot be delegated to an LLM . When you need to check in on the status of a project, or respond to someone else’s ping, or anything like that, you should compose and write the message yourself. Nothing will torch your relationship with other engineers as quickly as making them talk to your Claude Opus instance.

So where does that leave us? More or less where we were in 2024 , I think. Avoid at all costs becoming “the glue work person”, let bad processes fail so they can be changed, but be willing to do small amounts of tactical glue work where it can meaningfully contribute to the success of your projects. Most of your time and effort should still be spent on the code: on driving AI agents and aligning them with your company’s values .

- Glue work is all the squishy “non-technical” work that goes into building software: making sure teams are talking to each other, writing reports, updating docs, onboarding engineers, and so on. Specifically it’s the parts of that work that are not included in the formal process , and that only really get done if someone volunteers to do it. For more on why I don’t like it, see my 2024 post Glue work considered harmful . ↩

LLMs don’t know how to design software that uses LLMs. They’re comfortable writing normal programs, but if you throw an AI-shaped problem at them, they will usually screw it up. Why is that?

### Going down the symbolic rabbit hole

For example, this post describes an attempt to vibe-code a memory tool that would flag when one memory contradicted another 1 . This is a great instance of a task that was virtually impossible five years ago but is now relatively trivial due to LLMs. You can simply task a LLM with scanning for contradictions, either in a big batch or pairwise 2 .

However, when asked for the “state of the art” approach 3 , the AI agent in this case did not recommend LLMs. It started building a bewilderingly complex symbolic system to convert the memory items into structured logical atoms , then mechanically compare them with a solver. This, of course, did not and could not work, because there is no analytic way of determining whether any two natural-language sentences express the same proposition.

The LLM knew this was impossible! When the user eventually lost patience and said “hey, why isn’t this working”, Claude immediately explained that this was a known 130-year-old problem with no solution. And yet it happily went around and around for weeks iterating on a dead end.

I’ve run into this myself. When I was building Autodeck (AI-generated spaced repetition cards) my agents would routinely try to categorize cards by regex or keyword search instead of just making another LLM call.

### Why can’t LLMs use LLMs correctly?

Why would this be happening? I have two obvious explanations and one deeper one.

The first obvious explanation is that most training code is pre-LLMs . Assuming the labs aren’t feeding the current avalance of slop repositories directly into the models 4 , the vast majority of the code that models learn from was written before LLMs were an option. So it would make sense that they’d reach for non-LLM approaches, in the same way that they’d reach for jQuery over modern vanilla JS, or Backbone.js over React, right? Wrong, actually! LLMs don’t choose jQuery and Backbone. Whatever part of the training process pushes them towards up-to-date knowledge in other areas isn’t successfully pushing them towards LLMs, so this can’t be the whole story.

The second obvious explanation is that RLVR is not a good environment to write code that calls LLMs . Much of the time LLMs spend training is spent in reinforcement learning environments where an automatic grader determines their performance (for instance, by running some code they wrote and checking the outputs). I don’t know this for a fact, but I would be surprised if these environments contained the credentials and API access for a LLM to call other LLMs 5 . So even if the pretrained LLM was comfortable writing that kind of code, the reinforcement learning process might discourage 6 it from doing so.

The third explanation, which I like the most, is that current AI agents are just not very good at software design . On this explanation, picking a doomed symbolic approach instead of simply calling a LLM is not a weird aberration but a normal instance of AI agents picking the wrong tool for the job. I’ve seen this behavior from LLMs in other contexts too: trying to build complex (and doomed) consensus algorithms instead of tolerating stale data, introducing synchronous checks in event-driven systems, and so on. In the past I’ve chalked these up to alignment , but I’m open to the idea that they’re just ordinary errors of software design.

### Conclusion

One lesson I learn over and over again is that I can’t judge a LLM by the standards of a human. Any human programmer who was capable of implementing a sophisticated symbolic solver would know that it wouldn’t work, and so if they suggested that approach I’d assume 7 they had a good reason. Only a LLM could be both smart enough and dumb enough to make this mistake.

I write a lot about the skills that are involved in working effectively with LLMs. I still stand by what I wrote in February 2025 :

> Using LLMs well involves extracting value from what they’re good at and avoiding wasting time at what they’re bad at.

This is surprisingly hard, because of the point above. LLMs are good and bad seemingly at random: they will work hard for hours but sometimes be shockingly low-effort , they will draw on inhumanly broad expertise but fail to apply the most basic common-sense, they can successfully rewrite enormously complex programs but will often make very silly errors in design.

If you can predict where they will do well or badly ahead of time, you can get enormous value from LLMs; if you can’t, you will likely waste a lot of time and tokens going down hopeless approaches.

> What requirements don't you have? When designing software, the requirements you don’t have are as important as the requirements you do. Identifying what you can compromise on — what can be slow, or stale, or inflexible — is usually the key to an elegant design. For instance, take preforking web servers like Unicorn . Because they lack the feature of shared mutable state between server instances, they can run each server in its own process, which provides isolation for free.
